sources.title: A Bayesian phylogenetic study of the Kra-Dai language family
sources.note: Computational language-tree model proposes late-Holocene divergence and a southern-China dispersal area, while remaining a model rather than direct archaeological identification.

sources.title: Contrasting modes of cultural evolution: Kra-Dai languages and weaving technologies
sources.note: Compares language and loom histories and shows that technologies can spread across language communities rather than acting as ethnic fingerprints.

sources.title: Genetic structure of present-day Kra-Dai-speaking populations
sources.note: Modern genomes record mixture and later movements; the study discusses Tai-speaking southward expansion many centuries CE, not a 2000 BCE nation.

sources.title: Ancient DNA indicates human population shifts and admixture in northern and southern China
sources.note: Ancient genomes document changing ancestry and regional interaction, cautioning against equating genetic clusters with named languages.

sources.title: Ancient genomes reveal demographic history of coastal southern China
sources.note: Ancient DNA and archaeology show layered coastal population histories and later rice-farmer expansions, not a single timeless ethnolinguistic population.

sources.title: South and Island Southeast Asia: Languages
sources.note: Reference synthesis distinguishes language-family reconstruction, dispersal hypotheses and archaeological evidence across Southeast Asia.

sources.title: A Reference Grammar of Thai: historical excerpt
sources.note: Describes Thai and its written record, whose historical attestation belongs to the late second millennium CE rather than the Bronze Age.

sources.title: King Ram Khamhaeng Inscription nomination
sources.note: UNESCO documentation dates the famous Thai-language inscription to 1292 CE and identifies its Sukhothai setting.

sources.title: Formation of early states in the Central Plain: Erlitou and Erligang
sources.note: Archaeological synthesis of Erlitou urban planning, palatial compounds, craft production and the transition toward Erligang.

sources.title: Erlitou and the search for the Xia
sources.note: Explains why identifying the excavated Erlitou site directly with the later textual Xia dynasty remains contested.

sources.title: Rethinking Erlitou: legend, history and Chinese archaeology
sources.note: Separates excavated material sequences from much later historical traditions and nationalist master narratives.

sources.title: Radiocarbon dating of the Erlitou site
sources.note: Radiocarbon evidence refines Erlitou chronology and illustrates why approximate phases should not be treated as exact reign dates.

sources.title: Recent archaeometric research on the origins of Chinese civilisation
sources.note: Reviews radiocarbon, zooarchaeology, plant remains and material analyses that recover regional interaction without proving one identity.

sources.title: Mechanical treatments of bronzes and jades in ancient China
sources.note: Microscopic study of grinding and polishing includes Erlitou turquoise work and the labor embedded in elite composite objects.

sources.title: Institutions and Environment in Ancient Southern East Asia
sources.note: Regional synthesis covers Baodun, Chengdu Plain, Lower Yangzi, Maqiao, Erlitou networks and varied political institutions.

sources.title: Environmental Foundations to the Rise of Early Civilisations in China
sources.note: Multi-region synthesis relates settlement, rivers, flooding, cultivation and environmental change without environmental determinism.

sources.title: Site of Baodun yields earliest evidence for rice and foxtail millet in south-west China
sources.note: Flotation and seed identification show combined wetland rice and upland millet agriculture at Baodun.

sources.title: Shimao and Erlitou: origins of the bronze industry in central China
sources.note: Connects metal, jade and interaction evidence at two very different centers while emphasizing regional networks.

sources.title: Ancient genomes and pedigrees from Shimao
sources.note: Large ancient-DNA study reconstructs biological relationships and predominantly patrilineal descent among sampled people while examining sex-patterned sacrifice.

sources.title: Ancient mitochondrial genomes from Shimao
sources.note: Mitochondrial data show maternal-line diversity and affinity patterns; maternal lineages alone cannot define language, household or ethnicity.

sources.title: Bronze cultures of the northern frontiers during the early second millennium BCE
sources.note: Survey of distinctive northern and north-western metal traditions, mobility and exchange beyond Central Plain narratives.

sources.title: Animal management and diets in Bronze Age Hexi Corridor societies
sources.note: Stable-isotope analysis reveals varied fodder and grazing choices for sheep, goats, cattle, pigs and dogs at different sites.

sources.title: Sanxingdui archaeological site
sources.note: Institutional site history places an urban center at Sanxingdui from about 1800 BCE; its famous sacrificial bronze assemblages are largely later than this card.

sources.title: Agricultural diversification at Haimenkou, Yunnan
sources.note: Plant, animal and dating evidence records rice-millet farming, livestock and wild-resource use; directly dated wheat belongs after 1500 BCE.

sources.title: Morphometric approaches to Cannabis from Bronze Age Haimenkou, Yunnan
sources.note: The study’s site synthesis describes the initial 1600 to 1400 BCE occupation, pile-supported buildings, tools, a textile fragment and mixed subsistence.

sources.title: Southbound transmission of metallurgy: new excavations at Jicha in Yunnan
sources.note: Excavated metallurgical evidence situates Yunnan in long-distance technical transmission while distinguishing early and later phases.

sources.title: Food in Ancient China
sources.note: Archaeological synthesis emphasizes regional cuisines, cooking technology and unequal access rather than one national diet.

sources.title: Millet noodles in Late Neolithic China
sources.note: Microscopic study identifies a sealed bowl of long millet noodles at Lajia around 2000 BCE.

sources.title: Stable isotopes and dental caries reveal dietary change across ancient China
sources.note: Skeletal chemistry and teeth provide population-level clues to staple foods and oral health, with preservation and sampling limits.

sources.title: Parasitic infection on the Silk Road: latrine evidence
sources.note: Microscopy identifies parasite eggs in a much later historic latrine; its secure context shows why it cannot be projected back into this Bronze Age layer.

sources.title: Copper and bronze technology at Habaqila
sources.note: Laboratory study reveals alloying and production choices at a Lower Xiajiadian-related site, but the examined assemblage is later than 1500 BCE.

sources.title: Yin Xu archaeological site
sources.note: UNESCO documents late Shang oracle-bone inscriptions and the last capital, securely later than this card endpoint.

sources.title: The Archaeology of Early China
sources.note: Regional archaeological synthesis foregrounds changing settlements and interaction rather than a single linear civilization story.

sources.title: Millets, dogs, pigs and permanent settlement in Neolithic northern China
sources.note: Reviews millet productivity, settlement and integrated pig and dog husbandry while noting sparse plant and animal data.

sources.title: The origins and dispersal of rice cultivation
sources.note: Archaeobotanical review traces rice cultivation and dispersal while recording continuing chronological debate.

sources.title: Did crops expand with culinary practices?
sources.note: Ancient crop DNA and vessel evidence show that grains could travel without their original cooking traditions.

sources.title: The earliest rice domestication in China
sources.note: Review of rice remains and grain-identification debates cautions against treating every grain as proof of the same farming system.

sources.title: Variation of millet grain size and cooking techniques across Asia
sources.note: Comparative archaeobotany and vessel evidence distinguish boiling and steaming traditions from grinding and baking.

sources.title: Erlitou and the formation of Chinese civilization
sources.note: Study of Erlitou influence and elite culture also recognizes continuing regional diversity and selective adoption.

proposedOverrides.summary: A careful guide to the many Bronze Age communities hidden beneath the atlas’s anachronistic “Thai” label, separating language models from archaeology while exploring farms, homes, craft, families, health, sanitation and change from 2000 to 1500 BCE.
